slides.text: It started in a converted petrol station in Burlington, Vermont. It became one of the most values-driven brands on Earth.

In 1978, childhood friends Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield opened an ice cream shop with a $12,000 investment — nearly half of it borrowed. A decade later, President Reagan named them US Small Business Persons of the Year.
slides.footer: But the real story isn't the ice cream. It's what they did with the platform it gave them.

slides.text: When Pillsbury — owner of rival Häagen-Dazs — pressured shared distributors to drop Ben & Jerry's, the pair didn't sue quietly. They flew banners over Boston stadiums and printed an 800-number on their tubs: 'What's the Doughboy Afraid Of?'
It set the template for the next four decades: turn customer goodwill into pressure, and use the brand itself as an activism tool — on refugee support, LGBTQ+ rights, and climate justice.
slides.bold: the brand itself as an activism tool

slides.title: Most brands market their values. Ben & Jerry's spent decades acting on them.
bad: Adopts a cause when it's convenient
Drops it when it gets costly
good: Criticized the Iraq War and backed Occupy Wall Street — while under corporate ownership
Called to 'dismantle white supremacy' after George Floyd's murder
Built loyalty on shared values, not ad spend

slides.caption: In 2000, Unilever bought Ben & Jerry's for $326 million — on one unusual condition: a separate, independent board with legal authority over the brand's social mission, in perpetuity.
slides.note: Business schools held the structure up for years as a model for preserving a company's purpose after acquisition.

slides.text: But the brand's clearest reputation is for taking a stand on someone else's issue — war, politics, human rights. Its own core product tells a harder story.
slides.footer: Dairy farming is one of the largest sources of methane on the planet.

slides.callout: "It's a good question. I don't know."
slides.text: Asked directly whether Ben & Jerry's should tell customers plainly that milk and cream carry a real climate cost — the way it takes a stand on almost everything else — co-founder Ben Cohen gave a disarmingly honest answer.
slides.footer: It's not greenwashing — nothing is being misrepresented. But it's a real gap between a brand loud about Gaza or voting rights, and quieter about the emissions baked into its own best-selling product.

slides.caption: For nearly two decades, Ben & Jerry's 'Caring Dairy' programme has worked with farms in Vermont, the Netherlands, Germany and the UK on climate-smart practices and animal welfare — and it's since launched a full oat-based, non-dairy range as a lower-footprint alternative.
slides.footer: A real step. Not yet the plain admission that the flagship product has a cost worth confronting head-on.

slides.text: In 2021, Ben & Jerry's independent board voted to stop selling ice cream in the occupied West Bank. Unilever sold the local trademark instead. By 2025, the company's ice cream division was spun off into a new company, Magnum — and the founders' fight to keep the brand's voice intact went public.
slides.footer: Jerry Greenfield resigned from the board in 2025 — the first time in nearly 50 years he'd stepped away — writing that a company that can't stand up for what it believes 'isn't worth being a company at all.'

slides.text: Ben & Jerry's proves values-led business can build both loyalty and profit — Magnum reports over 9% growth even as the brand keeps picking fights. The real test of authenticity isn't the causes a brand is loud about. It's the ones closer to home.
